summary.text: Counting pairs divisible by each power of \(p\) and applying Legendre’s factorial formula gives \(v_p(a(m))=\sum_{i\ge1}\lfloor m/p^i\rfloor^2-\sum_{i,k\ge1}k\lfloor m/(kp^i)\rfloor\), with integrality following from \(\sum_k k\lfloor N/k\rfloor\le N^2\). If \(p\nmid M\), every quotient in these sums is unchanged when \(M\) is replaced by \(M-1\); iterating this adjacent equality from \(np\) through the next \(p-1\) integers proves the claim.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
N(m)=\prod_{j=1}^m\prod_{k=1}^m \gcd(j,k),
\qquad
D(m)=\prod_{k=1}^m \left(\left\lfloor\frac m k\right\rfloor!\right)^k.
\]
Thus the sequence in the statement is
\[
a(m)=\frac{N(m)}{D(m)}.
\]
We will first prove that this quotient is an integer and obtain an explicit formula for each of its prime-adic orders. We then show directly from that formula that the order at a prime \(p\) does not change when the argument is increased by one, except possibly at multiples of \(p\).

For a prime \(q\) and a positive integer \(x\), write \(v_q(x)\) for the exponent of \(q\) in \(x\).

First, for every positive integer \(d\), the number of multiples of \(d\) in \(\{1,\dots,m\}\) is
\[
\left\lfloor\frac m d\right\rfloor.
\]
Consequently, the number of ordered pairs \((j,k)\in\{1,\dots,m\}^2\) for which \(d\mid j\) and \(d\mid k\) is
\[
\left\lfloor\frac m d\right\rfloor^2.
\]

For fixed \(j,k\geq 1\), the exponent of \(q\) in their greatest common divisor can be counted one power at a time:
\[
v_q(\gcd(j,k))
 =\sum_{i\geq 1}{\bf 1}_{q^i\mid j\,\text{ and }\,q^i\mid k}.
\]
When \(j,k\leq m\), all terms with sufficiently large \(i\) vanish; in particular, it is enough to sum over \(1\leq i\leq m\), because a prime is at least \(2\), and \(q^i>m\) once \(i=m\) or beyond, apart from harmless zero terms. Summing over all ordered pairs and interchanging the finite sums gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_q(N(m))
&=\sum_{j=1}^m\sum_{k=1}^m v_q(\gcd(j,k))\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^m
  \#\{(j,k):1\leq j,k\leq m,\ q^i\mid j,\ q^i\mid k\}\\
&=\sum_{i=1}^m\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Define
\[
A_q(m):=\sum_{i=1}^m\left\lfloor\frac{m}{q^i}\right\rfloor^2.
\]
We have therefore shown
\[
v_q(N(m))=A_q(m). \tag{1}
\]

We next compute the exponent in the denominator. Legendre's formula says that, for every nonnegative integer \(r\),
\[
v_q(r!)=\sum_{i\geq 1}\left\lfloor\frac r{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Again, in the present situation the sum may be truncated at \(i=m\). Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_q(D(m))
&=\sum_{k=1}^m k\,v_q\!\left(\left\lfloor\frac m k\right\rfloor!\right)\\
&=\sum_{k=1}^m k\sum_{i=1}^m
  \left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/k\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\end{aligned}
\]
For positive integers \(k,q^i\), successive integer division satisfies
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{\lfloor m/k\rfloor}{q^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{m}{kq^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Interchanging the finite sums therefore yields
\[
v_q(D(m))
 =\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{k=1}^m
 k\left\lfloor\frac{m}{kq^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Set
\[
B_q(m):=\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{k=1}^m
 k\left\lfloor\frac{m}{kq^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
Thus
\[
v_q(D(m))=B_q(m). \tag{2}
\]

We now verify that \(D(m)\mid N(m)\), so that the displayed quotient defining \(a(m)\) is indeed exact. We use the elementary inequality
\[
\sum_{k=1}^m k\left\lfloor\frac Nk\right\rfloor\leq N^2 \tag{3}
\]
for arbitrary nonnegative integers \(N,m\). To see this, if \(k>N\), then \(\lfloor N/k\rfloor=0\). If \(k\leq N\), then
\[
k\left\lfloor\frac Nk\right\rfloor\leq N.
\]
There are at most \(N\) indices \(k\) with \(1\leq k\leq m\) and \(k\leq N\), so the whole sum is at most \(N\cdot N=N^2\).

Fix a prime \(q\) and an index \(i\), and put
\[
N_i=\left\lfloor\frac m{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
The same rule for successive integer division gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{m}{kq^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{N_i}{k}\right\rfloor.
\]
Applying (3) with \(N=N_i\), we obtain
\[
\sum_{k=1}^m k\left\lfloor\frac{m}{kq^i}\right\rfloor
 =\sum_{k=1}^m k\left\lfloor\frac{N_i}{k}\right\rfloor
 \leq N_i^2
 =\left\lfloor\frac m{q^i}\right\rfloor^2.
\]
Summing this inequality over \(i=1,\dots,m\) gives
\[
B_q(m)\leq A_q(m).
\]
By (1) and (2), this says
\[
v_q(D(m))\leq v_q(N(m))
\]
for every prime \(q\). Both products are positive, and comparison of all prime exponents therefore proves
\[
D(m)\mid N(m).
\]
It follows in particular that \(a(m)\) is a positive integer and
\[
v_q(a(m))=v_q(N(m))-v_q(D(m))=A_q(m)-B_q(m). \tag{4}
\]

The key step is now the following one-step invariance.

**Claim.** If \(M>0\), \(p\) is prime, and \(p\nmid M\), then
\[
v_p(a(M))=v_p(a(M-1)). \tag{5}
\]

We prove this by showing separately that both floor sums in (4) are unchanged.

We use the elementary fact that, for positive integers \(x,d\), if \(d\nmid x\), then
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{x}{d}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{x-1}{d}\right\rfloor. \tag{6}
\]
Indeed, decreasing an integer by one changes its quotient on division by \(d\) exactly when the original integer is divisible by \(d\).

Because \(p\nmid M\), no positive power \(p^i\), \(i\geq1\), divides \(M\). Applying (6) with \(d=p^i\) gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac M{p^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{M-1}{p^i}\right\rfloor
 \qquad(i\geq1). \tag{7}
\]
Thus every term of \(A_p(M)\) agrees with the corresponding term formed using \(M-1\). The only apparent difference between \(A_p(M)\) and \(A_p(M-1)\) is that the first sum includes the index \(i=M\). This extra term vanishes: since \(p\geq2\) and \(M>0\),
\[
p^M>M-1,
\]
so
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{M-1}{p^M}\right\rfloor=0.
\]
Therefore
\[
A_p(M)=A_p(M-1). \tag{8}
\]

For the denominator sum, observe first that no integer of the form \(kp^i\), with \(k\geq1\) and \(i\geq1\), can divide \(M\). If it did, then \(p\mid kp^i\mid M\), contrary to \(p\nmid M\). Hence (6) also gives
\[
\left\lfloor\frac M{kp^i}\right\rfloor
 =\left\lfloor\frac{M-1}{kp^i}\right\rfloor
 \qquad(k,i\geq1). \tag{9}
\]
Substituting this into the definition of \(B_p(M)\), we get
\[
B_p(M)=\sum_{i=1}^M\sum_{k=1}^M
 k\left\lfloor\frac{M-1}{kp^i}\right\rfloor. \tag{10}
\]
We may remove from this double sum all terms with \(k=M\), because
\[
Mp^i>M-1
\]
and hence \(\lfloor(M-1)/(Mp^i)\rfloor=0\). We may also remove all terms with \(i=M\): for every \(k\geq1\),
\[
kp^M\geq p^M>M-1,
\]
so these quotients are zero as well. What remains from (10) is exactly
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{M-1}\sum_{k=1}^{M-1}
 k\left\lfloor\frac{M-1}{kp^i}\right\rfloor
 =B_p(M-1).
\]
Thus
\[
B_p(M)=B_p(M-1). \tag{11}
\]
Combining (4), (8), and (11) proves the claim (5).

We now apply the claim throughout the desired block. Let \(n>0\), let \(p\) be prime, and let \(0\leq k<p\). For each integer \(r\) with
\[
1\leq r\leq k,
\]
the number \(np+r\) is not divisible by \(p\). Indeed, if \(p\mid np+r\), then, since \(p\mid np\), subtraction would give \(p\mid r\). But a positive multiple of \(p\) is at least \(p\), whereas \(1\leq r\leq k<p\), a contradiction.

Also \(np+r>0\), since \(n>0\) and \(p\geq2\). We may therefore apply (5) with \(M=np+r\), obtaining
\[
v_p(a(np+r))=v_p(a(np+r-1))
\qquad(1\leq r\leq k).
\]
Chaining these equalities gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_p(a(np+k))
&=v_p(a(np+k-1))\\
&=\cdots\\
&=v_p(a(np)).
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(k=0\) the equality is immediate, so this covers every \(k<p\). Therefore, for every positive integer \(n\), every prime \(p\), and every \(k\) with \(0\leq k<p\),
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np))=\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+k)).}
\]
Equivalently, \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np)),\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+1)),\ldots,\operatorname{ord}_p(a(np+p-1))\) are all equal, as claimed.
